summaries.example: Imagine a truth-checking game about the sentence “Every animal in the garden is quiet.” One player chooses an animal to test. The other must show that the chosen animal is quiet. If the first player can find a noisy animal, that player wins. The choices turn the sentence into a little contest, and a plan that always succeeds is a winning strategy.
summaries.summary: The entry explains how games became useful tools in logic. A logical game has players, rules for choosing, and rules for deciding who wins. A strategy is a plan for responding to the other player's moves; a winning strategy works against every response. In semantic games, the moves follow the shape of a sentence. For example, one player may choose an object for “every,” while the other chooses an object for “some.” A sentence is treated as true when the appropriate player has a winning strategy. Other games compare two mathematical structures: Spoiler tries to find a difference, while Duplicator tries to answer so that the structures continue to look alike. Games can also model imperfect information, movement through systems, building structures, and dialogue about proofs. The entry also asks an important question: if players are part of an explanation, what are they really trying to achieve? A game can clarify logic, but its players and goals should not be treated as automatically meaningful just because the game has winners and losers.
key_ideas: Logic and games are connected because both use rules, choices, and careful reasoning.
Logical games usually have two players, often called ∀ and ∃, who choose objects or follow instructions.
A winning strategy can act like a proof: it shows how to succeed no matter what the other player chooses.
Semantic games help explain truth in formal logic. Other games compare structures or describe proofs.
Some games have imperfect information, so a player must choose without knowing everything that happened earlier.
Back-and-forth games test whether two structures are alike in ways that a logical language can notice.
summaries.why_it_matters: Games give learners and researchers a clear picture of how logical claims work. They also connect logic with mathematics, computer science, teaching, debates, and the study of systems. A strategy can show not only that a claim succeeds, but how it succeeds step by step. Comparing games can reveal what different kinds of logic are able to express.

important_terms.definition: A rule-based activity in which players make choices and one player wins or loses.
A plan that tells a player what to do after every possible set of earlier moves.
A strategy that guarantees victory, whatever the other player does.
A game in which one player always has a winning strategy.
A game used to explain when a sentence is true by treating its parts as moves.

questions_to_think_about: Can a player have a plan that works even when the other player tries every possible move?
Why might turning a sentence into a game make its meaning easier to understand?
What could happen if a player is not allowed to know all the earlier moves?
How could a game compare two maps, machines, or other systems?

summaries.example: Consider two structures that represent networks. In a back-and-forth game, Spoiler selects a node in either network, and Duplicator selects a node in the other. Duplicator must preserve the relevant relationships among selected nodes. If Spoiler eventually exposes a relation that holds in one network but not the other, Spoiler wins. If Duplicator can respond successfully for every round, the two structures agree on the sentences that can be tested at that depth.
summaries.summary: The entry surveys the many ways games function in logic. A basic logical game specifies a domain of possible moves, whose turn it is at each position, and which finite positions or infinite plays count as wins. A strategy maps relevant positions to moves; a game is determined when one player has a winning strategy. Well-founded games are determined, but general infinite games need not be, and imperfect information can produce nondeterminacy even in a two-move game. In game-theoretic semantics, formulas become instructions for play. Quantifiers assign object-selection to different players, connectives assign choices, and negation can be represented by exchanging the players' roles. For first-order logic, this game interpretation agrees with Tarski-style truth under the stated mathematical assumptions, although the role of deterministic strategies and the axiom of choice is philosophically and mathematically significant. Games with imperfect information motivate logics involving independence and dependence, including team-based approaches. Modal and related logics use games on states and transitions, often allowing memoryless strategies. Back-and-forth games compare structures: Spoiler seeks a detectable mismatch, while Duplicator preserves a partial correspondence. Their finite-round versions measure what formulas of bounded complexity can distinguish, making them important in model theory and theoretical computer science. Forcing, cut-and-choose, automata, dialogue, and proof games extend the method further. Throughout, the entry cautions that the metaphor of opposing players does not by itself explain what a logical victory achieves.
key_ideas: Logical games differ from ordinary games: they often have two players, no chance, win-or-lose outcomes, and possibly infinitely many moves.

In semantic games for classical logic, the structure of a formula determines the moves. Conjunction gives the challenge to one player, disjunction gives a choice to the other, and quantifiers determine who selects an object.

For suitable first-order games, truth in a structure corresponds to the existence of a winning strategy for the designated player. The connection also raises questions about deterministic strategies and the axiom of choice.
Imperfect-information games show that even a short game may be undetermined: neither player needs to have a strategy that guarantees victory.
Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé, or back-and-forth, games compare structures and help characterize elementary equivalence and the expressive power of formal languages.

Other games build models, study definability and learning, connect logic with automata, or represent dialogue and proof. Their explanatory value depends partly on what the players' goals are supposed to mean.
summaries.why_it_matters: Game semantics links abstract logic to concrete procedures: choosing witnesses, answering challenges, preserving correspondences, and constructing models. This makes logical truth, equivalence, proof, and expressive power easier to analyze while revealing their differences. The same ideas support model theory, database and learning theory, computer-system verification, automata, and studies of reasoning under limited information. They also encourage philosophical care about whether a game's players and goals genuinely explain the concepts the game represents.

important_terms.definition: A formal system whose moves, turns, and winning conditions are specified mathematically.
A rule assigning each position in a game to the player who moves next.
A rule for choosing a move at every position where a particular player must act.
A strategy that wins against every possible strategy or response by the opponent.
A game in which at least one player has a winning strategy.
A game that explains truth by assigning choices to players as a formula is evaluated.
A game in which players may be restricted from using parts of the previous history.
A game in which one player challenges a structure and the other preserves matching relationships between two structures.

questions_to_think_about: Why does perfect information help establish determinacy, while limited information can prevent it?
Is a winning strategy best understood as a proof, a method of computation, or something else?
How many rounds of a back-and-forth game are needed to distinguish two structures?
What is gained, and what may be lost, when a logical concept is represented as a game?
Can rules for a proof dialogue explain the meaning of each step without already assuming a logic?

summaries.example: Suppose a sentence says, “For every kind of snack, there is a drink that goes with it.” In a simple semantic game, one player chooses a snack. The other must choose a drink that matches it. If the second player has a rule that works for every snack choice, the game treats the sentence as true in that setting. If the second player must choose without seeing some earlier choice, the result may change, because the player is no longer allowed to use all the information.
summaries.summary: The entry studies the relationship between formal logic and games. Logical games usually involve two players who choose elements from a domain according to a turn rule. A play can be finite or infinite, and the winning conditions determine whether a player wins. A strategy gives instructions for every relevant position; a winning strategy succeeds no matter how the opponent acts. Some games are determined, but infinite games and games with imperfect information need not be. Semantic games interpret formulas as contests. A player may choose an object for an existential claim, while the other challenges a universal claim; conjunctions and disjunctions similarly assign different choices. For classical first-order logic, the existence of a winning strategy can match truth in a structure. However, the entry notes that this match involves subtle issues about deterministic strategies and the axiom of choice. In imperfect-information games, a player may have to ignore earlier moves, and even a two-step game can lack a guaranteed winner. Back-and-forth games take a different approach: Spoiler tries to expose a difference between two structures, while Duplicator answers by preserving matching relationships. Winning strategies in bounded versions reveal what formulas of limited complexity can distinguish. The entry also surveys games for modal and other logics, model construction, definability, automata, proof, and dialogue. It repeatedly asks whether game players are genuine explanatory agents or simply useful mathematical roles.
key_ideas: Logic has used debates and games for a long time, both to teach reasoning and to study its rules.
In a semantic game, words such as “every,” “some,” “and,” and “or” can be represented by different players' choices.
A winning strategy explains how a logical claim can succeed against challenges, but the game metaphor does not automatically explain what the players are trying to accomplish.
Games with perfect information and games with imperfect information behave differently. Limited knowledge can make a short game have no guaranteed winner.
Back-and-forth games compare structures by asking whether one player can always match the other's moves without revealing a difference.
Logical games are also used to study modal systems, mathematical models, definability, computer science, and dialogue about proofs.
summaries.why_it_matters: Games turn logical ideas into visible patterns of challenge and response. They can show why a formula is true, why two structures cannot be distinguished by a language, or how a model can be built. These methods are useful in mathematics and computer science, including the analysis of programs, databases, formal languages, and systems. They also help students notice that changing information, rules, or goals can change what a logical statement means.

important_terms.definition: A formal contest with rules for turns, legal choices, and deciding which player wins.
A complete plan for responding to every position that could arise during a game.
A plan that guarantees a player's victory regardless of the opponent's choices.
A game in which one player or the other has a winning strategy.
A game that uses the parts of a sentence to decide who chooses and what counts as success.
A game where a player cannot use all information about earlier moves.
A game for comparing two structures by matching choices between them.
The idea that two structures satisfy exactly the same sentences in a chosen logic.

questions_to_think_about: Why might “every” be represented by a challenge, while “some” is represented by a choice?
Can a game be fair in its rules but still have no player with a guaranteed winning plan?
When two structures look the same in a game, what kind of sameness has really been shown?
Should a winning strategy count as a proof, or is it only a helpful picture of a proof?
Why might forgetting earlier moves change the logic of a game?
